paper_metadata.title: Informed Machine Learning - A Taxonomy and Survey of Integrating Prior Knowledge into Learning Systems
paper_metadata.venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
paper_metadata.abstract: Despite its great success, machine learning can have its limits when dealing with insufficient training data. A potential solution is the additional integration of prior knowledge into the training process which leads to the notion of informed machine learning. In this paper, we present a structured overview of various approaches in this field. We provide a definition and propose a concept for informed machine learning which illustrates its building blocks and distinguishes it from conventional machine learning. We introduce a taxonomy that serves as a classification framework for informed machine learning approaches. It considers the source of knowledge, its representation, and its integration into the machine learning pipeline. Based on this taxonomy, we survey related research and describe how different knowledge representations such as algebraic equations, logic rules, or simulation results can be used in learning systems. This evaluation of numerous papers on the basis of our taxonomy uncovers key methods in the field of informed machine learning.

paper_metadata.title: An Introduction to Deep Reinforcement Learning
paper_metadata.venue: Foundations and Trends® in Machine Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning is the combination of reinforcement learning (RL) and deep learning. This field of research has been able to solve a wide range of complex decision making tasks that were previously out of reach for a machine. Thus, deep RL opens up many new applications in domains such as healthcare, robotics, smart grids, finance, and many more. This manuscript provides an introduction to deep reinforcement learning models, algorithms and techniques. Particular focus is on the aspects related to generalization and how deep RL can be used for practical applications. We assume the reader is familiar with basic machine learning concepts.

paper_metadata.title: Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Intrusion Detection Systems: A Survey
paper_metadata.abstract: Networks play important roles in modern life, and cyber security has become a vital research area. An intrusion detection system (IDS) which is an important cyber security technique, monitors the state of software and hardware running in the network. Despite decades of development, existing IDSs still face challenges in improving the detection accuracy, reducing the false alarm rate and detecting unknown attacks. To solve the above problems, many researchers have focused on developing IDSs that capitalize on machine learning methods. Machine learning methods can automatically discover the essential differences between normal data and abnormal data with high accuracy. In addition, machine learning methods have strong generalizability, so they are also able to detect unknown attacks. Deep learning is a branch of machine learning, whose performance is remarkable and has become a research hotspot. This survey proposes a taxonomy of IDS that takes data objects as the main dimension to classify and summarize machine learning-based and deep learning-based IDS literature. We believe that this type of taxonomy framework is fit for cyber security researchers. The survey first clarifies the concept and taxonomy of IDSs. Then, the machine learning algorithms frequently used in IDSs, metrics, and benchmark datasets are introduced. Next, combined with the representative literature, we take the proposed taxonomic system as a baseline and explain how to solve key IDS issues with machine learning and deep learning techniques. Finally, challenges and future developments are discussed by reviewing recent representative studies.

paper_metadata.title: Training Spiking Neural Networks Using Lessons From Deep Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: The brain is the perfect place to look for inspiration to develop more efficient neural networks. The inner workings of our synapses and neurons provide a glimpse at what the future of deep learning might look like. This article serves as a tutorial and perspective showing how to apply the lessons learned from several decades of research in deep learning, gradient descent, backpropagation, and neuroscience to biologically plausible spiking neural networks (SNNs). We also explore the delicate interplay between encoding data as spikes and the learning process; the challenges and solutions of applying gradient-based learning to SNNs; the subtle link between temporal backpropagation and spike timing-dependent plasticity; and how deep learning might move toward biologically plausible online learning. Some ideas are well accepted and commonly used among the neuromorphic engineering community, while others are presented or justified for the first time here. A series of companion interactive tutorials complementary to this article using our Python package, snnTorch , are also made available: https://snntorch.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/index.html.

paper_metadata.title: Machine Learning and Deep Learning frameworks and libraries for large-scale data mining: a survey
paper_metadata.abstract: The combined impact of new computing resources and techniques with an increasing avalanche of large datasets, is transforming many research areas and may lead to technological breakthroughs that can be used by billions of people. In the recent years, Machine Learning and especially its subfield Deep Learning have seen impressive advances. Techniques developed within these two fields are now able to analyze and learn from huge amounts of real world examples in a disparate formats. While the number of Machine Learning algorithms is extensive and growing, their implementations through frameworks and libraries is also extensive and growing too. The software development in this field is fast paced with a large number of open-source software coming from the academy, industry, start-ups or wider open-source communities. This survey presents a recent time-slide comprehensive overview with comparisons as well as trends in development and usage of cutting-edge Artificial Intelligence software. It also provides an overview of massive parallelism support that is capable of scaling computation effectively and efficiently in the era of Big Data.

paper_metadata.title: Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Climate change is one of the greatest challenges facing humanity, and we, as machine learning experts, may wonder how we can help. Here we describe how machine learning can be a powerful tool in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and helping society adapt to a changing climate. From smart grids to disaster management, we identify high impact problems where existing gaps can be filled by machine learning, in collaboration with other fields. Our recommendations encompass exciting research questions as well as promising business opportunities. We call on the machine learning community to join the global effort against climate change.

paper_metadata.title: AI applications to medical images: From machine learning to deep learning
paper_metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: Artificial intelligence (AI) models are playing an increasing role in biomedical research and healthcare services. This review focuses on challenges points to be clarified about how to develop AI applications as clinical decision support systems in the real-world context. METHODS: A narrative review has been performed including a critical assessment of articles published between 1989 and 2021 that guided challenging sections. RESULTS: We first illustrate the architectural characteristics of machine learning (ML)/radiomics and deep learning (DL) approaches. For ML/radiomics, the phases of feature selection and of training, validation, and testing are described. DL models are presented as multi-layered artificial/convolutional neural networks, allowing us to directly process images. The data curation section includes technical steps such as image labelling, image annotation (with segmentation as a crucial step in radiomics), data harmonization (enabling compensation for differences in imaging protocols that typically generate noise in non-AI imaging studies) and federated learning. Thereafter, we dedicate specific sections to: sample size calculation, considering multiple testing in AI approaches; procedures for data augmentation to work with limited and unbalanced datasets; and the interpretability of AI models (the so-called black box issue). Pros and cons for choosing ML versus DL to implement AI applications to medical imaging are finally presented in a synoptic way. CONCLUSIONS: Biomedicine and healthcare systems are one of the most important fields for AI applications and medical imaging is probably the most suitable and promising domain. Clarification of specific challenging points facilitates the development of such systems and their translation to clinical practice.

paper_metadata.title: Machine learning and soil sciences: a review aided by machine learning tools
paper_metadata.abstract: Abstract. The application of machine learning (ML) techniques in various fields of science has increased rapidly, especially in the last 10 years. The increasing availability of soil data that can be efficiently acquired remotely and proximally, and freely available open-source algorithms, have led to an accelerated adoption of ML techniques to analyse soil data. Given the large number of publications, it is an impossible task to manually review all papers on the application of ML in soil science without narrowing down a narrative of ML application in a specific research question. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive review of the application of ML techniques in soil science aided by a ML algorithm (latent Dirichlet allocation) to find patterns in a large collection of text corpora. The objective is to gain insight into publications of ML applications in soil science and to discuss the research gaps in this topic. We found that (a) there is an increasing usage of ML methods in soil sciences, mostly concentrated in developed countries, (b) the reviewed publications can be grouped into 12 topics, namely remote sensing, soil organic carbon, water, contamination, methods (ensembles), erosion and parent material, methods (NN, neural networks, SVM, support vector machines), spectroscopy, modelling (classes), crops, physical, and modelling (continuous), and (c) advanced ML methods usually perform better than simpler approaches thanks to their capability to capture non-linear relationships. From these findings, we found research gaps, in particular, about the precautions that should be taken (parsimony) to avoid overfitting, and that the interpretability of the ML models is an important aspect to consider when applying advanced ML methods in order to improve our knowledge and understanding of soil. We foresee that a large number of studies will focus on the latter topic.

7.desc: Related-work RAG, 3 iterations, 1 neutral reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: The paper proposes a novel conceptual reformulation of de novo peptide sequencing as a mass prediction problem, moving beyond fixed token vocabularies and enabling zero-shot learning for unseen PTMs.
The work presents a thorough exploration of training strategies, including multi-task learning with simulated and experimental spectra, and the use of an adversarial loss for domain alignment.
The paper is well-written, clearly structured, and provides a candid and insightful discussion of limitations, results, and potential failure modes.
weaknesses: The central claim of zero-shot inference for unseen PTMs on experimental data is not convincingly supported, as the method shows minimal to no practical generalization in this setting.

Experimental evaluation on the main application domain (real spectra with unseen PTMs) is weak, with very low recall rates (e.g., 14% for methionine oxidation and ~3% for cysteine carbamidation) and unclear evidence of true zero-shot capability beyond memorizing similar seen masses.

weakness_details.weakness: The central claim of zero-shot inference for unseen PTMs on experimental data is not convincingly supported, as the method shows minimal to no practical generalization in this setting.
weakness_details.evidence: The paper explicitly states that performance on experimental spectra with unseen PTMs is 'inadequate' and 'remains limited' (Sections 4.2.2, 4.2.3). Figures 2B and 4C show predicted mass distributions for unseen residues with no clear peak at the correct mass for cysteine carbamidomethylation, and only a modest peak for methionine oxidation adjacent to a known amino acid (phenylalanine). Recall scores on these unseen residues are very low (0.6% to ~15%). The authors' rebuttal correctly points to these acknowledgements but does not present new evidence to refute the weakness.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The paper's main claim of enabling 'true open-search DNPS' and 'zero-shot inference for unseen residues, including novel PTMs' (Abstract, Introduction, main contributions).

weakness_details.weakness: Experimental evaluation on the main application domain (real spectra with unseen PTMs) is weak, with very low recall rates (e.g., 14% for methionine oxidation and ~3% for cysteine carbamidation) and unclear evidence of true zero-shot capability beyond memorizing similar seen masses.
weakness_details.evidence: The paper acknowledges that the performance on seen residues is lower than classification-based models (62.37% AA recall vs. Casanovo/AdaNovo). For unseen modifications, the recall for methionine oxidation is 14.41% and the authors note this 'perhaps reflected a memorization artifact' because its mass is nearly identical to phenylalanine's. The recall for cysteine carbamidomethylation is only 3.18%. The MTL models trained on simulation show Pearson correlations as low as 0.04 on experimental data (Section 4.2.2). The authors' rebuttal acknowledges these limitations and offers future directions, but does not change the assessment that the evaluation in the submitted paper is insufficient to support the claims.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The significance and practical utility of the proposed method for advancing de novo peptide sequencing for novel PTM discovery.

soundness.justification: The methodology is technically sound, but the central technical claim of effective zero-shot inference on experimental spectra is not supported by the evidence in the paper. The authors' rebuttal does not present new evidence to alter this assessment; it accepts the weakness and points to existing acknowledgements of the limitation. The failure is in validating the primary application.

novelty.justification: The reformulation of DNPS as continuous mass regression and the proposed training framework remains a novel and compelling idea. The rebuttal reinforces this conceptual contribution.

significance.justification: The authors' rebuttal frames the work as a 'conceptual framework' and 'foundation,' acknowledging the current limitations of practical performance. While the idea is significant, the demonstrated contribution in the submitted paper does not yet meaningfully advance the field beyond a proof of concept, as conceded by the authors themselves ('not solving zero-shot residue inference on experimental data').

evaluation.justification: The rebuttal confirms the concern regarding limited evaluation (e.g., teacher forcing only) and acknowledges the need for more extensive baseline comparisons. These promises for future work do not change the fact that the evaluation in the submitted paper is incomplete and does not convincingly support the claims. The low recall rates and poor generalization results stand.

presentation.justification: The paper remains clear and well-structured. The rebuttal does not alter this assessment.

reviewers.summary_comment: The authors' second rebuttal reinforces their position that this is foundational work and a proof of concept rather than a production-ready system. They correctly note that they have been transparent about limitations throughout the paper. However, this does not resolve the core weaknesses identified. The paper makes ambitious claims about enabling 'true open-search DNPS' and 'zero-shot inference for unseen residues' in the abstract and introduction, but the experimental results show minimal practical generalization capability on the target domain (experimental spectra with unseen PTMs). While the conceptual framework is indeed novel and the work represents an important first step, the evidence provided does not convincingly demonstrate that the approach works as claimed for its primary application. The modest improvements cited (e.g., cysteine recall increasing from 0.6% to 3.18%) remain far from practical utility and do not constitute convincing evidence of zero-shot capability. The paper would be stronger if it more carefully calibrated its claims to match the demonstrated results. As it stands, the work does not meet the standard for acceptance at a top-tier conference, though it represents a promising direction for future research.

why_it_fits: The paper proposes a novel reformulation of a biological sequence prediction problem (de novo peptide sequencing) as a mass regression task, which falls under 'general machine learning' and 'application-driven machine learning'.
It employs advanced deep learning techniques including transformers, multi-task learning, and adversarial training, which are core methodologies within ICML's scope.
The work addresses a clear limitation in proteomics (handling unseen post-translational modifications) through a machine learning lens, connecting to 'AI/ML for health and biotechnology'.
why_it_does_not_fit: Reviewer feedback indicates the central claim of zero-shot inference on experimental data is not convincingly supported, with 'minimal to no practical generalization'. ICML strongly values sound empirical validation of core claims.

The work is positioned as a proof-of-concept with limited practical performance (recall rates of 3-15% for target tasks). ICML typically expects more mature contributions with stronger empirical results.
The evaluation is noted as weak and incomplete (teacher forcing only, limited baseline comparisons). ICML places high emphasis on rigorous, comprehensive evaluation.

The reviewer states the 'significance' of the demonstrated contribution fails, as it does not yet meaningfully advance the field beyond a conceptual framework, which lowers its appeal for ICML's competitive standards.

why_it_fits: The paper fits directly within 'AI/ML for health and biotechnology', a highlighted topic area for NeurIPS.
The problem formulation—enabling zero-shot learning for novel biological entities—aligns with NeurIPS's interest in generalization and foundational learning challenges.
The methodology combines several popular NeurIPS themes: transformer architectures, adversarial domain alignment, and multi-task learning.
The paper includes a thorough NeurIPS checklist, discussing broader impacts, limitations, and reproducibility, meeting the conference's expectations for responsible research practices.
why_it_does_not_fit: The primary weakness, as highlighted by the reviewer, is that the core claim of zero-shot generalization on real data lacks convincing empirical support. NeurIPS is highly competitive and expects strong validation of novel claims.
The reviewer's assessment that the 'significance' gate fails because the work is more a proof-of-concept than a demonstrated advancement reduces its impact for a venue like NeurIPS.

While the conceptual idea is novel, the execution and evaluation are deemed insufficient by the reviewer ('Experimental evaluation on the main application domain... is weak'). NeurIPS typically requires stronger empirical evidence to support methodological innovations.
The paper's self-assessment as a 'foundation for future research' rather than a solved problem may make it a risky submission given NeurIPS's high bar for immediate contribution and impact.

why_it_fits: The work is fundamentally about representation learning for a specialized domain (mass spectrometry spectra to peptide sequences), aligning with ICLR's focus on 'representation learning for... other modalities'.
It heavily utilizes transformer architectures, a core deep learning model frequently featured at ICLR.
The problem involves learning continuous, generalizable representations (masses) instead of discrete tokens, which connects to ICLR's interests in novel representation paradigms within deep learning.
The use of simulated data for training and domain adaptation via adversarial learning touches on themes of data efficiency and generalization common at ICLR.
why_it_does_not_fit: The application domain (proteomics) is quite specific. While ICLR welcomes applications, the core deep learning contribution is judged against a very high bar, and the weak empirical results noted by the reviewer could be a major hurdle.
The reviewer's criticism regarding unsupported claims and weak evaluation on the primary task ('soundness' and 'evaluation' gates fail) is significant for ICLR, which emphasizes empirical rigor.

The method's novelty lies more in the problem reformulation for a specific field than in a fundamental advance to deep learning theory or architecture. ICLR often prioritizes work that pushes the boundaries of deep learning methodology itself.

The paper's admitted status as a proof-of-concept with teacher-forced evaluation only suggests it is an early-stage exploration, which may be less competitive at ICLR where more complete and validated deep learning studies are typical.

review.summary_comment: This paper addresses an important and challenging problem in proteomics: enabling de novo peptide sequencing to generalize to unseen post-translational modifications. The core idea of reformulating sequence prediction as continuous mass regression to enable zero-shot learning is novel and well-motivated. The paper is honest and insightful in its analysis of results and limitations. However, the experimental evaluation demonstrates that the method does not yet achieve its ambitious goal. Performance on real spectra with unseen PTMs is weak, and the practical utility remains a proof of concept. While the idea is promising and the exploration of multi-task and adversarial training is commendable, the current results do not meet the standard for a top-tier conference as they fail to convincingly support the central claim of enabling open-search DNPS. The work would benefit from stronger empirical validation, a full autoregressive decoding evaluation, and demonstration of clear advantages over or complementary benefits to existing approaches.

weakness_details.weakness: Experimental evaluation on the main application domain (real spectra with unseen PTMs) is weak, with very low recall rates (e.g., 14% for methionine oxidation and ~3% for cysteine carbamidation) and unclear evidence of true zero-shot capability beyond memorizing similar seen masses.
weakness_details.evidence: The paper acknowledges that the performance on seen residues is lower than classification-based models (62.37% AA recall vs. Casanovo/AdaNovo). For unseen modifications, the recall for methionine oxidation is 14.41% and the authors note this 'perhaps reflected a memorization artifact' because its mass is nearly identical to phenylalanine's. The recall for cysteine carbamidomethylation is only 3.18%. The MTL models trained on simulation show Pearson correlations as low as 0.04 on experimental data (Section 4.2.2). The authors' rebuttal acknowledges these limitations and offers future directions, but does not change the assessment that the evaluation in the submitted paper is insufficient to support the claims.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The significance and practical utility of the proposed method for advancing de novo peptide sequencing for novel PTM discovery.

soundness.justification: The methodology is technically sound, but the central technical claim of effective zero-shot inference on experimental spectra is not supported by the evidence in the paper. The authors' rebuttal does not present new evidence to alter this assessment; it accepts the weakness and points to existing acknowledgements of the limitation. The failure is in validating the primary application.

novelty.justification: The reformulation of DNPS as continuous mass regression and the proposed training framework remains a novel and compelling idea. The rebuttal reinforces this conceptual contribution.

significance.justification: The authors' rebuttal frames the work as a 'conceptual framework' and 'foundation,' acknowledging the current limitations of practical performance. While the idea is significant, the demonstrated contribution in the submitted paper does not yet meaningfully advance the field beyond a proof of concept, as conceded by the authors themselves ('not solving zero-shot residue inference on experimental data').

evaluation.justification: The rebuttal confirms the concern regarding limited evaluation (e.g., teacher forcing only) and acknowledges the need for more extensive baseline comparisons. These promises for future work do not change the fact that the evaluation in the submitted paper is incomplete and does not convincingly support the claims. The low recall rates and poor generalization results stand.

presentation.justification: The paper remains clear and well-structured. The rebuttal does not alter this assessment.

review.summary_comment: The authors' second rebuttal reinforces their position that this is foundational work and a proof of concept rather than a production-ready system. They correctly note that they have been transparent about limitations throughout the paper. However, this does not resolve the core weaknesses identified. The paper makes ambitious claims about enabling 'true open-search DNPS' and 'zero-shot inference for unseen residues' in the abstract and introduction, but the experimental results show minimal practical generalization capability on the target domain (experimental spectra with unseen PTMs). While the conceptual framework is indeed novel and the work represents an important first step, the evidence provided does not convincingly demonstrate that the approach works as claimed for its primary application. The modest improvements cited (e.g., cysteine recall increasing from 0.6% to 3.18%) remain far from practical utility and do not constitute convincing evidence of zero-shot capability. The paper would be stronger if it more carefully calibrated its claims to match the demonstrated results. As it stands, the work does not meet the standard for acceptance at a top-tier conference, though it represents a promising direction for future research.

target_paper_summary.title: Towards Open-Search De Novo Peptide Sequencing Via Mass-Based Zero-Shot Learning
target_paper_summary.abstract: 1 Proteins are the main drivers of biochemical processes and play a pivotal role in 2 almost all cellular functions. Through post-translational modifications (PTMs), 3 residues within a protein can be chemically modified to fine-tune the protein's 4 function in the cellular context. Despite the importance of PTMs, the plethora 5 of deep learning-based de novo peptide sequencing (DNPS) models, which, in 6 contrast to database searching approaches, predict peptide sequence solely from 7 tandem mass spectra without any reference organism database, can only predict 8 peptide sequences with a limited set of PTMs. This is because they rely on fixed 9 vocabularies that map residue tokens to non-generalizable learned embeddings. To 10 overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages the fact that 11 amino acids and their derivatives are characterized by their mass, a generalizable 12 feature that enables zero-shot learning. Specifically, we reformulate DNPS as a 13 mass prediction problem instead of a multiclass classification problem, where the 14 model predicts the mass of the next residue instead of its token representation. To 15 facilitate generalization to unseen PTMs, we leverage an adversarial multi-task 16 learning scheme by supplementing the training data of experimental spectra with 17 simulated spectra that mimic spectra containing unseen residues. We show that our 18 approach allows the prediction of previously unseen PTMs, providing a promising 19 proof of concept for mass-based representations as a path towards true open-search 20 DNPS.
claims: we propose a novel approach that leverages the fact that 11 amino acids and their derivatives are characterized by their mass, a generalizable 12 feature that enables zero-shot learning.
We show that our 18 approach allows the prediction of previously unseen PTMs, providing a promising 19 proof of concept for mass-based representations as a path towards true open-search 20 DNPS.

paper_metadata.title: Predicting glycan structure from tandem mass spectrometry via deep learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Glycans constitute the most complicated post-translational modification, modulating protein activity in health and disease. However, structural annotation from tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) data is a bottleneck in glycomics, preventing high-throughput endeavors and relegating glycomics to a few experts. Trained on a newly curated set of 500,000 annotated MS/MS spectra, here we present CandyCrunch, a dilated residual neural network predicting glycan structure from raw liquid chromatography-MS/MS data in seconds (top-1 accuracy: 90.3%). We developed an open-access Python-based workflow of raw data conversion and prediction, followed by automated curation and fragment annotation, with predictions recapitulating and extending expert annotation. We demonstrate that this can be used for de novo annotation, diagnostic fragment identification and high-throughput glycomics. For maximum impact, this entire pipeline is tightly interlaced with our glycowork platform and can be easily tested at https://colab.research.google.com/github/BojarLab/CandyCrunch/blob/main/CandyCrunch.ipynb . We envision CandyCrunch to democratize structural glycomics and the elucidation of biological roles of glycans.

paper_metadata.title: Opportunities and obstacles for deep learning in biology and medicine
paper_metadata.abstract: Abstract Deep learning, which describes a class of machine learning algorithms, has recently showed impressive results across a variety of domains. Biology and medicine are data rich, but the data are complex and often ill-understood. Problems of this nature may be particularly well-suited to deep learning techniques. We examine applications of deep learning to a variety of biomedical problems—patient classification, fundamental biological processes, and treatment of patients—and discuss whether deep learning will transform these tasks or if the biomedical sphere poses unique challenges. We find that deep learning has yet to revolutionize or definitively resolve any of these problems, but promising advances have been made on the prior state of the art. Even when improvement over a previous baseline has been modest, we have seen signs that deep learning methods may speed or aid human investigation. More work is needed to address concerns related to interpretability and how to best model each problem. Furthermore, the limited amount of labeled data for training presents problems in some domains, as do legal and privacy constraints on work with sensitive health records. Nonetheless, we foresee deep learning powering changes at both bench and bedside with the potential to transform several areas of biology and medicine.

paper_metadata.title: Prediction of glycopeptide fragment mass spectra by deep learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Deep learning has achieved a notable success in mass spectrometry-based proteomics and is now emerging in glycoproteomics. While various deep learning models can predict fragment mass spectra of peptides with good accuracy, they cannot cope with the non-linear glycan structure in an intact glycopeptide. Herein, we present DeepGlyco, a deep learning-based approach for the prediction of fragment spectra of intact glycopeptides. Our model adopts tree-structured long-short term memory networks to process the glycan moiety and a graph neural network architecture to incorporate potential fragmentation pathways of a specific glycan structure. This feature is beneficial to model explainability and differentiation ability of glycan structural isomers. We further demonstrate that predicted spectral libraries can be used for data-independent acquisition glycoproteomics as a supplement for library completeness. We expect that this work will provide a valuable deep learning resource for glycoproteomics.

paper_metadata.title: Deep learning and generative methods in cheminformatics and chemical biology: navigating small molecule space intelligently
paper_metadata.abstract: The number of 'small' molecules that may be of interest to chemical biologists - chemical space - is enormous, but the fraction that have ever been made is tiny. Most strategies are discriminative, i.e. have involved 'forward' problems (have molecule, establish properties). However, we normally wish to solve the much harder generative or inverse problem (describe desired properties, find molecule). 'Deep' (machine) learning based on large-scale neural networks underpins technologies such as computer vision, natural language processing, driverless cars, and world-leading performance in games such as Go; it can also be applied to the solution of inverse problems in chemical biology. In particular, recent developments in deep learning admit the in silico generation of candidate molecular structures and the prediction of their properties, thereby allowing one to navigate (bio)chemical space intelligently. These methods are revolutionary but require an understanding of both (bio)chemistry and computer science to be exploited to best advantage. We give a high-level (non-mathematical) background to the deep learning revolution, and set out the crucial issue for chemical biology and informatics as a two-way mapping from the discrete nature of individual molecules to the continuous but high-dimensional latent representation that may best reflect chemical space. A variety of architectures can do this; we focus on a particular type known as variational autoencoders. We then provide some examples of recent successes of these kinds of approach, and a look towards the future.

paper_metadata.title: Diffusion models in bioinformatics and computational biology
xTrimoPGLM: Unified 100B-Scale Pre-trained Transformer for Deciphering the Language of Protein
paper_metadata.abstract: Protein language models have shown remarkable success in learning biological information from protein sequences. However, most existing models are limited by either autoencoding or autoregressive pre-training objectives, which makes them struggle to handle protein understanding and generation tasks concurrently. We propose a unified protein language model, xTrimoPGLM, to address these two types of tasks simultaneously through an innovative pre-training framework. Our key technical contribution is an exploration of the compatibility and the potential for joint optimization of the two types of objectives, which has led to a strategy for training xTrimoPGLM at an unprecedented scale of 100 billion parameters and 1 trillion training tokens. Our extensive experiments reveal that 1) xTrimoPGLM significantly outperforms other advanced baselines in 18 protein understanding benchmarks across four categories. The model also facilitates an atomic-resolution view of protein structures, leading to an advanced 3D structural prediction model that surpasses existing language model-based tools. 2) xTrimoPGLM not only can generate de novo protein sequences following the principles of natural ones, but also can perform programmable generation after supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on curated sequences. These results highlight the substantial capability and versatility of xTrimoPGLM in understanding and generating protein sequences, contributing to the evolving landscape of foundation models in protein science. Trained weight for the xTrimoPGLM model, and downstream datasets are available at https://huggingface.co/proteinglm .

paper_metadata.title: Exploration of cell state heterogeneity using single-cell proteomics through sensitivity-tailored data-independent acquisition
paper_metadata.abstract: Single-cell resolution analysis of complex biological tissues is fundamental to capture cell-state heterogeneity and distinct cellular signaling patterns that remain obscured with population-based techniques. The limited amount of material encapsulated in a single cell however, raises significant technical challenges to molecular profiling. Due to extensive optimization efforts, single-cell proteomics by Mass Spectrometry (scp-MS) has emerged as a powerful tool to facilitate proteome profiling from ultra-low amounts of input, although further development is needed to realize its full potential. To this end, we carry out comprehensive analysis of orbitrap-based data-independent acquisition (DIA) for limited material proteomics. Notably, we find a fundamental difference between optimal DIA methods for high- and low-load samples. We further improve our low-input DIA method by relying on high-resolution MS1 quantification, thus enhancing sensitivity by more efficiently utilizing available mass analyzer time. With our ultra-low input tailored DIA method, we are able to accommodate long injection times and high resolution, while keeping the scan cycle time low enough to ensure robust quantification. Finally, we demonstrate the capability of our approach by profiling mouse embryonic stem cell culture conditions, showcasing heterogeneity in global proteomes and highlighting distinct differences in key metabolic enzyme expression in distinct cell subclusters.

7.desc: Related-work RAG, 3 iterations, 1 neutral reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: Proposes a novel and interesting idea of applying consistency distillation to diffusion-based sampling from unnormalized densities, enabling single-step inference.
Presents a comprehensive algorithmic framework with two distinct methods (CDDS and SCDS), including a training procedure that does not require pre-collected datasets.
Provides extensive empirical evaluation on a diverse set of synthetic and real-world benchmarks, demonstrating significant computational savings (reduced NFEs) compared to strong baselines.
weaknesses: The novelty claim of single-step sampling for unnormalized distributions is somewhat diminished by the existence of consistency models and distillation techniques in generative modeling; the core adaptation to sampling without data is incremental.

The empirical results for the more practical SCDS method (which requires no pretrained teacher) show that its single-step performance is often weaker than the teacher-dependent CDDS and sometimes worse than multi-step baselines, raising questions about its significance for top-tier conferences.
The theoretical analysis is limited to a single theorem concerning the distillation error for CDDS, with no theoretical guarantees provided for the more complex and novel SCDS method.

weakness_details.weakness: The novelty claim of single-step sampling for unnormalized distributions is somewhat diminished by the existence of consistency models and distillation techniques in generative modeling; the core adaptation to sampling without data is incremental.
weakness_details.evidence: The rebuttal argues that solving sampling without data is a 'new problem' and that the proposed algorithms are 'novel algorithmic solutions'. However, the submitted paper's technical core—using a consistency loss on trajectories from a diffusion process and conditioning a network on step size—remains an application of established consistency principles to a different objective function (sampling vs. data generation). The conceptual leap of applying these tools to a density-only setting, while practically useful, does not constitute a fundamental methodological innovation on the level expected for a top-tier venue.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The central claim of introducing a new class of samplers for single-step generation from unnormalized densities.

weakness_details.weakness: The empirical results for the more practical SCDS method (which requires no pretrained teacher) show that its single-step performance is often weaker than the teacher-dependent CDDS and sometimes worse than multi-step baselines, raising questions about its significance for top-tier conferences.
weakness_details.evidence: The rebuttal reframes significance around providing a 'new capability' and a 'Pareto frontier'. However, the submitted results (Table 1, Figure 3) substantiate the original concern: the autonomous SCDS's one-step quality is frequently non-competitive. While it provides a flexible trade-off, the fact that its quality at the most ambitious operating point (single-step) is often lacking relative to standard methods indicates the contribution's practical impact is currently limited to niche high-throughput, lower-fidelity scenarios. This does not meet the threshold for a significant advancement in the core problem of high-quality sampling.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The claim that SCDS 'delivers competitive sample quality while drastically reducing sampling steps' and its significance as a meaningful advancement.

soundness.justification: Unchanged. The technical derivation and experimental evaluation remain sound.

novelty.justification: The rebuttal does not introduce new evidence from the submission to alter the assessment. The work successfully applies and extends existing consistency concepts to a new problem setting. While this represents a solid contribution, it is an incremental adaptation of known techniques rather than a breakthrough in methodology or theory.

significance.justification: The rebuttal's argument about establishing a 'new Pareto frontier' is undercut by the submitted data. The frontier demonstrated shows a clear trade-off where high efficiency comes at a cost to sample quality on challenging benchmarks. For a top-tier conference, a significant advance in sampling would typically require pushing the Pareto frontier outward—improving quality at a given cost or reducing cost without compromising quality. The submitted results show SCDS expands the frontier primarily along the cost axis at the expense of quality, which is a valuable but more incremental engineering contribution.

evaluation.justification: Unchanged. The evaluation is comprehensive.

presentation.justification: Unchanged. The paper is well-written.

reviewers.summary_comment: The author rebuttal provides a spirited defense, correctly emphasizing the practical challenges addressed and the utility of the proposed methods. However, it does not resolve the fundamental concerns about novelty and significance for a top-tier venue. The work is a competent and well-engineered application of consistency-model ideas to the problem of sampling from unnormalized densities. It delivers genuine computational benefits, especially for high-throughput scenarios. Nonetheless, the conceptual foundation is adapted from prior work, and the performance of the more general SCDS method involves a significant quality trade-off that limits its impact as a definitive advance in high-fidelity sampling. Therefore, while a valuable contribution to the literature, it does not meet the high acceptance bar.

why_it_fits: The paper's core focus is on efficient sampling from unnormalized distributions, which is a fundamental and well-established topic within machine learning, aligning with ICML's scope in general machine learning, probabilistic methods, and optimization.

It proposes new algorithmic methods (CDDS, SCDS) that improve the computational efficiency of diffusion-based samplers, which fits ICML's interest in machine learning systems, improved implementation, and scalability.
The methodology is empirically driven with extensive evaluations on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, which is a strong positive for ICML's emphasis on rigorous empirical evaluation.
why_it_does_not_fit: Reviewer 1's major criticism questions the fundamental novelty, describing the work as an 'incremental adaptation' of existing consistency model principles to a new objective. This is a significant risk for ICML, which highly values clear and substantial methodological novelty.

The reviewer notes the theoretical analysis is limited to a single theorem for CDDS, with no guarantees for the more novel SCDS. ICML has a strong theory track, and a lack of theoretical grounding for the primary contribution could be a liability.

While empirically sound, the significance is questioned because the more practical SCDS method's single-step performance is often weaker than baselines. ICML looks for work with clear, significant impact, and a trade-off between speed and quality might be seen as an incremental engineering contribution rather than a paradigm shift.

why_it_fits: NeurIPS has a strong and broad focus on deep learning, generative models, and optimization, all of which are central to this paper's technical approach of distilling and training diffusion models for sampling.

The paper tackles a practical bottleneck (high inference cost) in a widely-used class of models (diffusion samplers). NeurIPS welcomes contributions that improve the efficiency and applicability of AI/ML methods, aligning with interests in SysML infrastructure and AI/ML for physical/biological sciences.

The submission includes a thorough NeurIPS checklist, demonstrating careful attention to reproducibility, ethics, and societal impact, which aligns well with the conference's recent emphasis on responsible research practices.
why_it_does_not_fit: Similar to ICML, the primary risk stems from the reviewer's assessment of novelty and significance. NeurIPS also expects high novelty; the reviewer's conclusion that it is a 'competent and well-engineered application' of existing ideas rather than a breakthrough could limit its appeal.

The reviewer explicitly states the contribution does not meet the 'high acceptance bar' for a top-tier venue, citing concerns that the rebuttal did not resolve. This directly signals a high risk of rejection at NeurIPS if similar reviews are received.

The paper's contribution is primarily algorithmic and empirical. While this is welcome at NeurIPS, the lack of stronger theoretical results or a more dramatic empirical improvement (as noted by the reviewer on SCDS's quality trade-off) might place it in a highly competitive mid-tier range.

why_it_fits: ICLR's primary focus is deep learning and representation learning. This paper's core methodology is built entirely on deep neural networks parameterizing diffusion/consistency models, making it an excellent topical fit.

The work is directly situated within the literature on diffusion models and generative models (a core ICLR area), extending concepts like consistency models and distillation to the specific problem of sampling from unnormalized densities.

ICLR often values clear, well-executed algorithmic innovations and empirical demonstrations in deep learning. The paper's straightforward extension of consistency training to a new context and its comprehensive experiments align well with this culture, even if the conceptual leap is considered incremental by some reviewers.
why_it_does_not_fit: The problem setting—sampling from unnormalized densities—while applicable, is not the most central problem in ICLR, which tends to focus more on generative modeling *with data*. The paper's positioning in the 'sampling' literature might slightly dilute its direct relevance to the main ICLR audience.

The theoretical component is light. While ICLR is empirically focused, a stronger theoretical connection to the properties of the learned consistency function or the convergence of SCDS could have strengthened the submission.

The reviewer's criticism regarding the novelty of adapting existing techniques still applies, though ICLR might be slightly more forgiving of solid engineering advances within the deep learning paradigm compared to ICML or NeurIPS.

soundness.justification: The paper builds on established diffusion sampling and consistency model frameworks. novelty.justification: While the application context (sampling from unnormalized densities without data) is specific, the core technical ideas—distilling a multi-step sampler into a single-step one and using a self-consistency loss—are direct adaptations of established concepts from consistency models and progressive distillation in generative modeling. The step of conditioning the control on a step size is a non-trivial but incremental extension.

significance.justification: The practical benefit of the more autonomous SCDS method is questionable, as its one-step performance is often not competitive with multi-step baselines on several benchmarks. The computational savings, while substantial for large sample counts, come at a cost in sample quality for the method that does not rely on a pre-trained teacher, limiting its impact for high-stakes applications requiring high-fidelity samples.

evaluation.justification: The experimental evaluation is thorough, using multiple standard benchmarks (synthetic and real-world) and metrics (Sinkhorn distance, ESS, log Z error, ELBO). Comparisons are made against relevant state-of-the-art diffusion samplers. The analysis of computational cost (NFE) is convincing.

presentation.justification: The paper is generally well-written and clearly structured. Algorithms and figures are helpful for understanding the proposed methods. The exposition of the core ideas is accessible.

review.summary_comment: This paper presents a technically sound and well-evaluated approach for accelerating diffusion samplers via consistency distillation. The idea of enabling single-step sampling from unnormalized densities is appealing. However, the novelty is limited as it primarily adapts existing consistency training ideas to a new context. The work is a solid incremental contribution but does not meet the high bar for acceptance due to these limitations.

Existing sampling algorithms typically 3 require many iterative steps to produce high-quality samples, leading to high com4 putational costs that limit their practicality in time-sensitive or resource-constrained 5 settings. In this work, we introduce *consistent diffusion samplers*, a new class 6 of samplers designed to generate high-fidelity samples in a single step. paper_metadata.title: Random walks and diffusion on networks
paper_metadata.abstract: Random walks are ubiquitous in the sciences, and they are interesting from both theoretical and practical perspectives. They are one of the most fundamental types of stochastic processes; can be used to model numerous phenomena, including diffusion, interactions, and opinions among humans and animals; and can be used to extract information about important entities or dense groups of entities in a network. Random walks have been studied for many decades on both regular lattices and (especially in the last couple of decades) on networks with a variety of structures. In the present article, we survey the theory and applications of random walks on networks, restricting ourselves to simple cases of single and non-adaptive random walkers. We distinguish three main types of random walks: discrete-time random walks, node-centric continuous-time random walks, and edge-centric continuous-time random walks. We first briefly survey random walks on a line, and then we consider random walks on various types of networks. We extensively discuss applications of random walks, including ranking of nodes (e.g., PageRank), community detection, respondent-driven sampling, and opinion models such as voter models.

paper_metadata.title: Novel View Synthesis with Diffusion Models
paper_metadata.abstract: We present 3DiM, a diffusion model for 3D novel view synthesis, which is able to translate a single input view into consistent and sharp completions across many views. The core component of 3DiM is a pose-conditional image-to-image diffusion model, which takes a source view and its pose as inputs, and generates a novel view for a target pose as output. 3DiM can generate multiple views that are 3D consistent using a novel technique called stochastic conditioning. The output views are generated autoregressively, and during the generation of each novel view, one selects a random conditioning view from the set of available views at each denoising step. We demonstrate that stochastic conditioning significantly improves the 3D consistency of a naive sampler for an image-to-image diffusion model, which involves conditioning on a single fixed view. We compare 3DiM to prior work on the SRN ShapeNet dataset, demonstrating that 3DiM's generated completions from a single view achieve much higher fidelity, while being approximately 3D consistent. We also introduce a new evaluation methodology, 3D consistency scoring, to measure the 3D consistency of a generated object by training a neural field on the model's output views. 3DiM is geometry free, does not rely on hyper-networks or test-time optimization for novel view synthesis, and allows a single model to easily scale to a large number of scenes.

paper_metadata.title: Multilevel sequential Monte Carlo samplers
The drift diffusion model as the choice rule in reinforcement learning
Variance Reduction Using Nonreversible Langevin Samplers
paper_metadata.abstract: A standard approach to computing expectations with respect to a given target measure is to introduce an overdamped Langevin equation which is reversible with respect to the target distribution, and to approximate the expectation by a time-averaging estimator. As has been noted in recent papers [30, 37, 61, 72], introducing an appropriately chosen nonreversible component to the dynamics is beneficial, both in terms of reducing the asymptotic variance and of speeding up convergence to the target distribution. In this paper we present a detailed study of the dependence of the asymptotic variance on the deviation from reversibility. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical simulations.

paper_metadata.title: Preparation and performance features of wristband samplers and considerations for chemical exposure assessment
paper_metadata.venue: Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology
paper_metadata.abstract: Wristbands are increasingly used for assessing personal chemical exposures. Unlike some exposure assessment tools, guidelines for wristbands, such as preparation, applicable chemicals, and transport and storage logistics, are lacking. We tested the wristband's capacity to capture and retain 148 chemicals including polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), pesticides, flame retardants, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and volatile organic chemicals (VOCs). The chemicals span a wide range of physical-chemical properties, with log octanol-air partitioning coefficients from 2.1 to 13.7. All chemicals were quantitatively and precisely recovered from initial exposures, averaging 102% recovery with relative SD ≤21%. In simulated transport conditions at +30 °C, SVOCs were stable up to 1 month (average: 104%) and VOC levels were unchanged (average: 99%) for 7 days. During long-term storage at -20 °C up to 3 (VOCs) or 6 months (SVOCs), all chemical levels were stable from chemical degradation or diffusional losses, averaging 110%. Applying a paired wristband/active sampler study with human participants, the first estimates of wristband-air partitioning coefficients for PAHs are presented to aid in environmental air concentration estimates. Extrapolation of these stability results to other chemicals within the same physical-chemical parameters is expected to yield similar results. As we better define wristband characteristics, wristbands can be better integrated in exposure science and epidemiological studies.

paper_metadata.title: Exact and Computationally Efficient Likelihood-Based Estimation for Discretely Observed Diffusion Processes (with Discussion)
paper_metadata.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B (Statistical Methodology)
paper_metadata.abstract: Summary The objective of the paper is to present a novel methodology for likelihood-based inference for discretely observed diffusions. We propose Monte Carlo methods, which build on recent advances on the exact simulation of diffusions, for performing maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimation.

paper_metadata.title: Organic aerosol and global climate modelling: a review
paper_metadata.abstract: Abstract. The present paper reviews existing knowledge with regard to Organic Aerosol (OA) of importance for global climate modelling and defines critical gaps needed to reduce the involved uncertainties. All pieces required for the representation of OA in a global climate model are sketched out with special attention to Secondary Organic Aerosol (SOA): The emission estimates of primary carbonaceous particles and SOA precursor gases are summarized. The up-to-date understanding of the chemical formation and transformation of condensable organic material is outlined. Knowledge on the hygroscopicity of OA and measurements of optical properties of the organic aerosol constituents are summarized. The mechanisms of interactions of OA with clouds and dry and wet removal processes parameterisations in global models are outlined. This information is synthesized to provide a continuous analysis of the flow from the emitted material to the atmosphere up to the point of the climate impact of the produced organic aerosol. The sources of uncertainties at each step of this process are highlighted as areas that require further studies.

paper_metadata.title: Planck2013 results. XVI. Cosmological parameters
paper_metadata.abstract: This paper presents the first cosmological results based on Planck measurements of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature and lensing-potential power spectra. We find that the Planck spectra at high multipoles ( > 40) are extremely well described by the standard spatiallyflat six-parameter CDM cosmology with a power-law spectrum of adiabatic scalar perturbations. Within the context of this cosmology, the Planck data determine the cosmological parameters to high precision: the angular size of the sound horizon at recombination, the physical densities of baryons and cold dark matter, and the scalar spectral index are estimated to be * = (1.04147 0.00062) 10 -2 , b h 2 = 0.02205 0.00028, c h 2 = 0.1199 0.0027, and n s = 0.9603 0.0073, respectively (note that in this abstract we quote 68% errors on measured parameters and 95% upper limits on other parameters). For this cosmology, we find a low value of the Hubble constant, H 0 = (67.3 1.2) km s -1 Mpc -1 , and a high value of the matter density parameter, m = 0.315 0.017. These values are in tension with recent direct measurements of H 0 and the magnituderedshift relation for Type Ia supernovae, but are in excellent agreement with geometrical constraints from baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) surveys. Including curvature, we find that the Universe is consistent with spatial flatness to percent level precision using Planck CMB data alone. We use high-resolution CMB data together with Planck to provide greater control on extragalactic foreground components in an investigation of extensions to the six-parameter CDM model. We present selected results from a large grid of cosmological models, using a range of additional astrophysical data sets in addition to Planck and high-resolution CMB data. None of these models are favoured over the standard six-parameter CDM cosmology. The deviation of the scalar spectral index from unity is insensitive to the addition of tensor modes and to changes in the matter content of the Universe. We find an upper limit of r 0.002 < 0.11 on the tensor-to-scalar ratio. There is no evidence for additional neutrino-like relativistic particles beyond the three families of neutrinos in the standard model. Using BAO and CMB data, we find N eff = 3.30 0.27 for the effective number of relativistic degrees of freedom, and an upper limit of 0.23 eV for the sum of neutrino masses. Our results are in excellent agreement with big bang nucleosynthesis and the standard value of N eff = 3.046. We find no evidence for dynamical dark energy; using BAO and CMB data, the dark energy equation of state parameter is constrained to be w = -1.13 +0.13 -0.10 . We also use the Planck data to set limits on a possible variation of the fine-structure constant, dark matter annihilation and primordial magnetic fields. Despite the success of the six-parameter CDM model in describing the Planck data at high multipoles, we note that this cosmology does not provide a good fit to the temperature power spectrum at low multipoles. The unusual shape of the spectrum in the multipole range 20 < < 40 was seen previously in the WMAP data and is a real feature of the primordial CMB anisotropies. The poor fit to the spectrum at low multipoles is not of decisive significance, but is an "anomaly" in an otherwise self-consistent analysis of the Planck temperature data.

The black-box experiments use an external judge (Claude) or simple CoT prompts. weakness_details.evidence: Experiments are limited. White-box results (Table 1) are based on "three attack variations of an image" with high standard errors. Black-box evaluation on Attack-Bard (Table 2) presents accuracy numbers without error bars or statistical tests, and the dataset is small (200 images). The paper fails to conduct a rigorous, large-scale evaluation with multiple base models across a spectrum of robustness and with direct scaling of compute akin to Zaremba et al. 2025. Key claims like 'rich-get-richer' dynamics are based on sparse, noisy data.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The empirical validation of the RICH hypothesis and the conclusion that inference-time compute acts as an 'effective defense multiplier'.

soundness.justification: The central claim - that inference-time compute synergistically benefits robustness more for robust models - is not technically supported. The main experimental proxy (text repetition K) is not a valid substitute for reasoning-based compute scaling. The evidence is weak: low sample sizes (e.g., only 3 runs for white-box results), high variance, and lack of a direct comparison to compute scaling as defined in prior work. The causal link suggested by the hypothesis is not convincingly demonstrated with the provided experiments.

novelty.justification: The core observation - that the effectiveness of test-time defenses may depend on base model robustness - is not new. Prior work on adversarial training already shows that robust models force attacks into more interpretable, potentially in-distribution, regimes (Gaziv et al., 2023; Bartoldson et al., 2024). The paper synthesizes this idea with the recent finding on inference-time compute. The specific hypothesis (RICH) reframes known concepts but is not a distinct technical or conceptual advance. The RAG evidence also shows extensive prior work on robustness and scaling, though it does not directly connect the two.

significance.justification: The potential impact is limited by the questionable validity of the core experimental methodology. Even if the hypothesis were correct, the findings are presented at a small scale and with unconvincing simulations of inference-time compute. For a top-tier ML conference, the work does not provide a substantial advance in understanding or methodology for adversarial robustness.
significance.affected_claim: The claim that the work meaningfully clarifies how to improve robustness in exchange for inference-time compute.

evaluation.justification: The experiments do not adequately support the central claims. The primary proxy for compute scaling is flawed. The evaluation lacks statistical rigor (e.g., missing confidence intervals on key results like Table 2). The baselines and comparisons are insufficient (e.g., not comparing directly with the 'o1-v' style reasoning the paper critiques in Figure 2). The experiments on general attack targets (Section 4.3) are not comprehensive enough to support the broad conclusion that RICH holds across images and targets.

presentation.justification: The paper is clearly written and well-structured. The hypothesis is stated plainly, and the experimental setup is described in detail. Figures help illustrate the concepts. The work is sufficiently clear to permit assessment, which reveals the underlying methodological weaknesses.

review.summary_comment: This paper proposes the Robustness from Inference Compute Hypothesis (RICH), positing that the benefits of inference-time compute for adversarial robustness scale with a model's base robustness. While the idea is interesting and well-explained, the paper fails to provide convincing technical support. The crucial weakness is the experimental methodology: scaling inference-time compute via textual repetition ('K') is an inadequate proxy for the reasoning-based compute scaling studied in prior work. The empirical evidence is thin, with small-scale experiments, high variance, and insufficient statistical analysis. The central claim is therefore not substantiated. Furthermore, the underlying observation connecting robustness and interpretable attacks is not novel. The paper's clarity is a strength but does not compensate for its major flaws in soundness, novelty, and evaluation.

target_paper_summary.title: Get Rich Or Die Scaling: Profitably Trading Inference Compute For Robustness
target_paper_summary.abstract:
1 Recent work shows that increasing inference-time compute through generation of 2 long reasoning traces improves not just capability scores, but robustness to various 3 text jailbreaks designed to control models or lower their guardrails. However, 4 multimodal reasoning offers comparatively little defense against vision jailbreaks, 5 which typically succeed by creating noise-like perturbations. When attacking a 6 robust model, vision attacks are also capable of and often must resort to producing 7 human-interpretable perturbations. Rather than operating in a model's blind-spot 8 or out of its training distribution, such interpretable attacks construct familiar 9 concepts connected to the attacker's goal. Inspired by the ability of robust models 10 to force attacks into this space that appears more in-distribution for reasoning tasks, 11 we posit the Robustness from Inference Compute Hypothesis (RICH): defending 12 against attacks with inference compute (like reasoning) profits as those attacks 13 become more in-distribution. To test this, we adversarially attack models of varying 14 robustness with black-box-transfer and white-box attacks. RICH predicts a rich15 get-richer dynamic: models that start with higher initial robustness gain more 16 robustness benefits from increases in inference-time compute. Consistent with 17 RICH, we find that robust models benefit more from increased compute, whereas 18 non-robust models show little to no improvement. Our work suggests that inference19 time compute can be an effective defense against adversarial attacks, provided 20 the base model has some degree of robustness. In particular, layering disparate 21 train-time and test-time defenses aids robustness not additively, but synergistically.

Figure 1: **As model robustness increases, the benefits of inference-time compute on robustness** also increase. A red dot indicates the step at which the model first generates the output targeted by the PGD attack. Robustness increases from LLaVA-v1.5 to FARE-LLaVA-v1.5 to Delta2LLaVA-v1.5.

paper_metadata.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI): Multidisciplinary perspectives on emerging challenges, opportunities, and agenda for research, practice and policy
paper_metadata.abstract: As far back as the industrial revolution, significant development in technical innovation has succeeded in transforming numerous manual tasks and processes that had been in existence for decades where humans had reached the limits of physical capacity. Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers this same transformative potential for the augmentation and potential replacement of human tasks and activities within a wide range of industrial, intellectual and social applications. The pace of change for this new AI technological age is staggering, with new breakthroughs in algorithmic machine learning and autonomous decision-making, engendering new opportunities for continued innovation. The impact of AI could be significant, with industries ranging from: finance, healthcare, manufacturing, retail, supply chain, logistics and utilities, all potentially disrupted by the onset of AI technologies. The study brings together the collective insight from a number of leading expert contributors to highlight the significant opportunities, realistic assessment of impact, challenges and potential research agenda posed by the rapid emergence of AI within a number of domains: business and management, government, public sector, and science and technology. This research offers significant and timely insight to AI technology and its impact on the future of industry and society in general, whilst recognising the societal and industrial influence on pace and direction of AI development.

paper_metadata.title: Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures (with comments and a rejoinder by the author)
paper_metadata.abstract: There are two cultures in the use of statistical modeling to reach conclusions from data. One assumes that the data are generated by a given stochastic data model. The other uses algorithmic models and treats the data mechanism as unknown. The statistical community has been committed to the almost exclusive use of data models. This commitment has led to irrelevant theory, questionable conclusions, and has kept statisticians from working on a large range of interesting current problems. Algorithmic modeling, both in theory and practice, has developed rapidly in fields outside statistics. It can be used both on large complex data sets and as a more accurate and informative alternative to data modeling on smaller data sets. If our goal as a field is to use data to solve problems, then we need to move away from exclusive dependence on data models and adopt a more diverse set of tools.

paper_metadata.title: Anticompetitive Effects of Common Ownership
paper_metadata.abstract: ABSTRACT Many natural competitors are jointly held by a small set of large institutional investors. In the U.S. airline industry, taking common ownership into account implies increases in market concentration that are 10 times larger than what is “presumed likely to enhance market power” by antitrust authorities. Within‐route changes in common ownership concentration robustly correlate with route‐level changes in ticket prices, even when we only use variation in ownership due to the combination of two large asset managers. We conclude that a hidden social cost—reduced product market competition—accompanies the private benefits of diversification and good governance.

paper_metadata.title: The Value of Connections in Turbulent Times: Evidence from the United States
Is ChatGPT a General-Purpose Natural Language Processing Task Solver?
paper_metadata.abstract: Spurred by advancements in scale, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated the ability to perform a variety of natural language processing (NLP) tasks zero-shot—i.e., without adaptation on downstream data. Recently, the debut of ChatGPT has drawn a great deal of attention from the natural language processing (NLP) community due to the fact that it can generate high-quality responses to human input and self-correct previous mistakes based on subsequent conversations. However, it is not yet known whether ChatGPT can serve as a generalist model that can perform many NLP tasks zero-shot. In this work, we empirically analyze the zero-shot learning ability of ChatGPT by evaluating it on 20 popular NLP datasets covering 7 representative task categories. With extensive empirical studies, we demonstrate both the effectiveness and limitations of the current version of ChatGPT. We find that ChatGPT performs well on many tasks favoring reasoning capabilities (e.g., arithmetic reasoning) while it still faces challenges when solving specific tasks such as sequence tagging. We additionally provide in-depth analysis through qualitative case studies.

paper_metadata.title: Death by Market Power: Reform, Competition, and Patient Outcomes in the National Health Service
paper_metadata.abstract: The effect of competition on the quality of health care remains a contested issue. Most empirical estimates rely on inference from nonexperimental data. In contrast, this paper exploits a procompetitive policy reform to provide estimates of the impact of competition on hospital outcomes. The English government introduced a policy in 2006 to promote competition between hospitals. Using this policy to implement a difference-in-differences research design, we estimate the impact of the introduction of competition on not only clinical outcomes but also productivity and expenditure. We find that the effect of competition is to save lives without raising costs. (JEL H51, I11, I18, L32, L33)

paper_metadata.title: Bio-inspired computation: Where we stand and what's next
Why is Pollution from U.S. Manufacturing Declining? The Roles of Environmental Regulation, Productivity, and Trade
paper_metadata.abstract: Between 1990 and 2008, air pollution emissions from U.S. manufacturing fell by 60 percent despite a substantial increase in manufacturing output. We show that these emissions reductions are primarily driven by within-product changes in emissions intensity rather than changes in output or in the composition of products produced. We then develop and estimate a quantitative model linking trade with the environment to better understand the economic forces driving these changes. Our estimates suggest that the implicit pollution tax that manufacturers face doubled between 1990 and 2008. These changes in environmental regulation, rather than changes in productivity and trade, account for most of the emissions reductions.

strengths: Proposes a unified framework (AH-UGC) that addresses two key limitations of existing graph coarsening methods: lack of adaptivity (single pass for multiple ratios) and lack of semantic handling for heterogeneous graphs via type-isolated coarsening.
Demonstrates significant scalability improvements and computational efficiency, with extensive experiments on 23 diverse datasets (homophilic, heterophilic, heterogeneous, large-scale).
Provides theoretical guarantees regarding locality preservation (Theorem 3.1) and load balance (Theorem 3.2), linking the LSH and consistent hashing framework to the desired coarsening properties.
weaknesses: The core methodological innovation is an incremental combination of existing techniques (LSH from UGC and consistent hashing), with insufficient justification for why this specific combination is uniquely suited or optimal for the stated goals.

The experimental evaluation, while broad, has critical flaws. The node classification results (e.g., Table 3) show inconsistent and sometimes inferior performance compared to baselines like UGC, especially on heterophilic graphs, undermining claims of effectiveness and robustness.

The presentation of the method and algorithms is convoluted and contains unclear notation and definitions that hinder understanding, particularly around the coarsening matrix construction, heterophily factor α, and the interplay between modules.

weakness_details.weakness: The core methodological innovation is an incremental combination of existing techniques (LSH from UGC and consistent hashing), with insufficient justification for why this specific combination is uniquely suited or optimal for the stated goals.
weakness_details.evidence: The rebuttal again fails to resolve this concern. It reiterates the existing technical foundation (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 1) but concedes that a 'direct comparison to other adaptive strategies (e.g., dynamic binning) is absent' from the submitted paper. The argument that CH offers 'inherent load balancing' does not justify its suitability for locality-preserving coarsening over other strategies. The promised future discussion does not change the fact that the submitted work lacks this critical justification, leaving the novelty feeling incremental rather than fundamentally justified.
weakness_details.affected_claim: Claims of a novel, unified framework that is the first to support adaptive and heterogeneous coarsening.

weakness_details.weakness: The experimental evaluation, while broad, has critical flaws. The node classification results (e.g., Table 3) show inconsistent and sometimes inferior performance compared to baselines like UGC, especially on heterophilic graphs, undermining claims of effectiveness and robustness.
weakness_details.evidence: The rebuttal partially addresses this by agreeing to revise the claim of 'superior accuracy' to 'competitive accuracy.' However, this is an admission that the original claim in the submitted paper is unsupported. The evidence in Tables 3 and 8 remains unchanged: AH-UGC frequently performs similarly to or worse than UGC (e.g., PubMed-SAGE: 72.16 vs 87.34; many GIN results). While the efficiency gain is clear, the paper's overarching claim of advancing the state-of-the-art in coarsening effectiveness for downstream tasks is not met. The rebuttal's focus on enabling new applications does not alter the experimental results presented; it merely promises to reframe them.
weakness_details.affected_claim: Claims that AH-UGC 'consistently outperforms existing methods in scalability, classification accuracy, and structural fidelity' and demonstrates 'superior capacity to coarsen heterogeneous graphs while preserving their semantic and structural fidelity.'

soundness.justification: The central claim regarding effectiveness for downstream learning tasks remains unsound.
